idea.body: Every place in a decimal number is worth ten times the place to its right: ones, then tenths, then hundredths, then thousandths. In 4.283, the 2 is worth 2 tenths (0.2), the 8 is worth 8 hundredths (0.08), and the 3 is worth 3 thousandths (0.003). A digit further right is always worth less, no matter how big the digit itself looks. That is also why more digits does not mean a bigger decimal. 0.199 has three digits after the point, but it is still smaller than 0.5. Five tenths beats one tenth before any other digit matters.

figure.alt: A grid of 10 rows and 10 columns with 8 squares shaded, showing the digit 8 worth 8 hundredths, or 0.08.

workedExample.prompt: A kitchen scale reads 4.283 kilograms. What is the value of the digit 8 in that reading?
steps: Count the places right from the decimal point: 2 is tenths, 8 is hundredths, 3 is thousandths.
The digit 8 sits in the hundredths place.
A digit in the hundredths place is worth that digit times one hundredth.
8 times one hundredth is 0.08.

figure.alt: A grid of 10 rows and 10 columns with 8 squares shaded, showing the digit 8 worth 8 hundredths, or 0.08.

ways.name: Place value chart
ways.when: Use this when you need to name exactly what one digit in a decimal is worth.
steps: Count the places right from the decimal point: first tenths, then hundredths, then thousandths.
Find which place your digit sits in.
Multiply the digit by that place's value.
Write the result as a decimal.
ways.trap: Counting the ones digit as the first place after the point instead of starting with tenths.

ways.name: Expanded form
ways.when: Use this when splitting the whole decimal into a sum makes one piece easy to read off.
steps: Break the decimal into a sum of its places: ones, tenths, hundredths, thousandths.
Write each place as its own decimal piece, using a zero for any empty place.
Match your digit to the piece it came from.
That piece is the digit's value.
ways.trap: Forgetting the zero placeholder for an empty tenths place, which shifts every piece after it.

ways.name: Hundredths grid picture
ways.when: Use this when seeing the digit as shaded squares makes its size clear.
steps: Draw a 10 by 10 grid; each small square is one hundredth of the whole.
Find the digit and the place it sits in.
Turn that place value into a count of hundredths, then shade that many squares.
The shaded squares show the digit's value out of one whole.
ways.trap: Shading only 2 squares because the digit itself is 2, instead of 20 squares for 2 tenths.

figure.alt: A bar of 10 equal tenths with 2 shaded, showing the digit 2 in 3.29 is worth 2 tenths, 0.20.

frames.caption: Each small square is one hundredth.
Find the digit and its place.
Turn the place value into hundredths.
Shaded squares show the digit's value.

ways.name: Leftmost difference
ways.when: Use this when you need to tell which of two decimals is bigger, not just a digit's value.
steps: Line up both decimals by place, tenths under tenths, hundredths under hundredths.
Pad the shorter decimal with zeros so both reach the same length.
Compare the digits from left to right and stop at the first place where they differ.
The bigger digit at that place makes the bigger decimal.
ways.trap: Thinking 0.362 is bigger because it has more digits after the point.
